name: Adam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of a small depot up the valley, six of us covering about four hundred square miles of farmland and forest. Most of the job is overhead lines on wooden poles: trees falling on wires, a pole hit by a tractor, a fuse blown on a transformer up a farm track. I like that every day's different and you know every farmer by name. What wears me out is the winter callouts, driving icy roads at three in the morning to find a line down in a field.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like when you're not on call?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet. I rent a stone cottage at the end of Mill Lane with my dog, Bruno, and I spend weekends fishing or messing about with an old motorbike. I've got about two months' money saved, maybe a bit more. I'm not a computer person. I've got the phone the company gave me and I use it for calls and the work app, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Nothing up the valley ever changes that fast anyway. I'd probably just shrug at the pub and say the trees still fall on the lines and somebody's still got to go up and clear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. My job's not on a computer, it's on a pole in a wet field. The only thing that bothers me is the talk about closing our depot and running us out of the town one, and that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and try to build my savings up from two months to four. I'd keep my head down about the depot merger and hope it goes away. If it doesn't, I'd look at the other two electricity firms nearby, but I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit uneasy about the depot, but that was already there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the depot that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, the merger. If they close the valley depot, I'd have a forty-minute drive each way and I'd lose the call-out bonus for living close. That's about a tenth of my pay gone, just like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the people who were sure AI would change everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, you were wrong, no harm done. I'm not one for gloating. Most people were just guessing, same as me.

say: He'd shrug at the pub: **trees still fall** on the lines.
Somebody still has to go up and **clear them**, whatever AI does.
think: His job is on a pole in a **wet field**, not a computer.
The real worry is the **depot merger**, which has nothing to do with AI.
do: Carry on as normal and grow savings from **two to four months**.
Keep his head down and hope the **merger** goes away.
Look at the **other two firms** nearby only if he must.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a background unease about the depot.
S0.quote: My job's not on a computer, it's on a pole in a wet field.
fieldNote: His **pre-existing worry** is the depot merger and losing a call-out bonus.
He avoids conflict and **won't gloat**, typical of his centre outlook.
He prefers to **wait and hope** rather than act early.

steps.text: Keep working the valley depot rota as usual
Build savings from two months to four
Wait for news on the depot merger before job hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that should worry, not us. Planning, ordering, all that's going to change, but you still need someone to drive up the track and climb. I'd say it to anyone who asked, but I wouldn't go posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it makes the merger more likely. If software can plan the jobs from the town depot, why keep a little office up the valley? So my job's probably safe, but my nice local setup isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor straight out whether the depot's staying. If it's closing, I'd ask about keeping the call-out bonus. I'd keep saving, and I'd put off buying a new van for the motorbike stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, just a bad feeling in my stomach about the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says planning and booking go to software. How does that touch your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I imagine it'll send me jobs one after another with no say from me. Right now our supervisor, Graham, knows I'm quick on the forest lines and slow on the farms with dogs. Software won't know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the work app on your phone get more demanding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably wants more photos and more ticking. I'd do the minimum, honestly. I'm not going to learn a whole new system unless they make me.

say: The **office** should worry, not the crews who climb.
Someone still has to **drive up the track** and climb the pole.
think: Software planning from town makes the **depot merger** more likely.

do: Ask his supervisor **straight out** whether the depot stays.
Ask to keep the **call-out bonus** if it closes.
Put off buying a **new van** and keep saving.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a bad feeling about the depot.
S1.quote: If software can plan the jobs from the town depot, why keep a little office up the valley?
fieldNote: He links AI to the **merger** rather than to his own skills.
He'd do the **bare minimum** on new apps, true to his resistance.
He values **local knowledge** that software won't have.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor directly whether the valley depot stays open
Delay buying a van and keep saving monthly
Keep the old routine and do only the required app updates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it, that's what I'd say at work. A robot on an icy farm track at three in the morning? But I wouldn't be as sure as I sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2031 I'd be finished. I'd be thirty-one, with no other trade, and I've never touched these computer things. The office stuff goes in 2028, so the depot closes first, and then the robots finish the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd stop spending on the motorbike and save everything I can. I'd probably look into getting my heavy vehicle licence, so at least I can drive something. Beyond that I honestly wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm being straight with you. Lying awake listening to Bruno snore, thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots that can do hands-on work by 2031. What does that mean for the valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The valley would be the last place they'd send robots, I think. All those farm tracks, the mud, the trees. But last isn't never. Maybe 2032, 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not change firms. Would that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd take anything that's going. If the other firms are hiring anyone, I'd go. I'd even move to town, though I'd hate it.

A robot on an **icy farm track** at night sounds unlikely to him out loud.
think: He expects to be **finished by 2031**, at thirty-one.
He has **no other trade** and has never used AI tools.
do: Stop spending on the **motorbike** and save everything.
Look into a **heavy vehicle licence** as a fallback.
Apply to **any firm** hiring, even if it means moving to town.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake while his dog snores.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one, with no other trade, and I've never touched these computer things.
fieldNote: His public doubt **hides real fear** in private.
The **remote valley** gives him a little extra time, but not much.
He has **no plan** beyond a heavy vehicle licence.

steps.text: Stop spending on the motorbike and save everything possible
Get a heavy vehicle driving licence
Apply to the other two electricity firms nearby
Move to town if that's where the work is

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing as before at work, probably. I'd say five years is a long time and anything could happen. I don't want to be the guy at the pub who goes on about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to save and maybe learn something else, but I'd still be thirty-four when the robots come. My gut says the valley's last on the list, which might give me an extra year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, aiming for six months put by in the next three years. I'd do the heavy vehicle licence first, then maybe a course in underground cables, since digging in tight spots seems hard for a robot. And I'd keep an eye on the merger news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more of a slow worry. I can sleep, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years until AGI, eight until robots. What does that extra time buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time means I don't have to panic. With five years I can learn one thing properly, not three badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably let my mate Jonny, who's good with that stuff, show me the basics. I don't fancy it, but I'd rather learn from him than from a company video.

Let his mate Jonny show him **AI basics**.

steps.text: Save until six months of expenses are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and I've got a job now. I'd probably not say much at all, to be honest. People who predict ten years ahead are usually wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years means I can just carry on for a good while. I'd be forty when the robots come, still working, but with time to plan. Maybe it never comes. That's what I'd tell myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving, slowly. I'd probably do the heavy vehicle licence at some point, just in case. Otherwise I'd wait and see how it goes over the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but it's far enough away that I don't think about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd put the robots to the back of my mind. That's probably a mistake, but it's what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still up the valley, with a dog and a fishing rod. Maybe driving a truck for the robot crew, if that's what's left.

fieldNote: Ten years lets his **resistance** turn into postponement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, definitely. I've got no other trade and only two months saved. What would help is the company training us for whatever comes next, on paid time, and keeping a depot up the valley so I don't have to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the places like ours. Everyone talks about cities. Up the valley, if the depot goes, the farmers wait six hours for power instead of one.

headlineQuote: Up the valley, if the depot goes, the farmers wait six hours for power instead of one.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old lineworker at a **small valley depot** covering farms and forest.
He lives alone with his dog **Bruno**, with about two months saved.
He avoids computers and **waits and hopes** rather than act early.
His standing worry is a **depot merger**, which AI planning would speed up.
He fears **AGI by 2028** most, but postpones worry when given ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as he has no other trade and little savings.
